newsitem.title: USA: Credit card late payments at record high.
newsitem.headline: Credit card late payments at record high.

text.p: The buy-now-pay-later generation is getting into deeper water as late payments on credit cards jumped to a record high in the second quarter.

The American Bankers Association said Tuesday that credit card delinquencies were 3.66 percent of the total number of credit card accounts that were active between April and June, up from 3.53 percent in the first three months of the year.

The credit card delinquency ratio was the highest since the ABA began collecting data in 1974 and it was the seventh straight quarterly increase. The previous peak was in the first quarter of 1991 when it reached 3.34 percent.
A loan is considered delinquent when it is 30 days or more overdue.
Americans owed $454 billion in credit card debt at end of July, which represented 39 percent of all consumer lending, and it was up 18.8 percent from $382 billion at the same last year, the ABA said.
The delinquency rate, which the banking association blames on looser bank lending standards, is expected to worsen further before it improves.
"I would expect that we'll see delinquencies continue to rise somewhat over the next couple of quarters," James Chessen, the ABA's chief economist, said.

"The good news is that both consumers and lenders have begun to take steps to counter the rise in delinquencies," he added. Consumers are still taking on more debt but at a slower pace than in the past, he said.
"My sense is we're starting to see the peak of the debt burden levels," Chessen said.
Late payments for auto loans made through auto dealers rose to 2.48 percent in the second quarter from 2.13 percent.
That helped boost the ratio of delinquencies for eight types of consumer instalment loans to 2.32 percent at the end of the second quarter, up from 2.14 percent, the ABA said.
"The delinquencies being seen today are the result of lending decisions made by banks 18 to 24 months ago," Chessen said.
Banks are making an effort to tighten loan standards, but it will take time before that is reflected in the delinquency ratios, the ABA said.
"Issuers are cutting back on riskier credit card lending programmes, lowering credit limits, lengthening the time between automatic credit limit increases," Chessen said.
The pace of bank consumer lending was virtually flat with a 0.7 percent increase in the first seven months of this year, the ABA said.
"Although loan demand is still strong, consumer borrowing is likely to slow partly due to higher interest rates and banks' tightening of lending standards," the ABA report said.
The economy is expected to slow down in the second half of the year and the consumer debt burden may pinch spending slightly, economists said.
"The job market is much more important, and with jobs still growing, that says the consumer is still in good shape," said Stuart Hoffman, chief economist at PNC Bank Corp.
Even if the Federal Reserve were to raise interest rates next week as some economists believe, it would have little impact on the ability of consumers to pay off their credit card debt.
The average credit card balance is about $1,700, so even if rates moved up by a quarter of a percentage point, that would add about $4, Chessen said.
